## Introduction

Anthropogenic global changes linked to land-use change, resource exploitation, climate change, invasive alien species, and pollution pose major and accelerating threats to biodiversity and ecosystem functioning [@Ipbes2019-sd]. These global change drivers do not act in isolation, however, but occur simultaneously and often interact in complex ways so that their cumulative impacts may exceed the sum of single drivers [@Komatsu2019-yr; @oliver2014interactions; @Speiser2022-st; @xue2024number]. While these interactive effects are complex, understanding such interactions is key to forecasting changes to biodiversity exposed to multiple global change drivers. Experiments are one way to disentangle the effects of complex interactions and providing a mechanistic understanding of the multifactorial nature of global change drivers.

This need has inspired numerous experiments manipulating multiple global change drivers simultaneously [@dainese2024global; @Komatsu2019-yr; @rillig2019role]. One insight from these experiments is that different drivers often impact plant community biomass, as well as plant species composition and diversity (see @fig-concept a; @borer2024planning; @collins2022global; @kaarlejarvi2017herbivores; @post2008opposing; @proulx1998reversal; @Speiser2022-st; @zhou2020responses). One of the major mechanisms through which several of these drivers, including warming and nitrogen addition, are affecting plant community composition and diversity, is through increased community biomass resulting in more competitive interactions for light and nutrients [@chesson2000mechanisms; @grime1973competitive]. An increase in standing biomass in response to warming, nitrogen addition or both can thus shift the intensity of the dominant plant-plant interactions and may lead to communities with taller, faster growing and denser vegetation sward which are stronger competitors for light and nutrients, while lower-stature and slower growing specialist species decreasing in abundance and diversity [@Alexander2015-gu; @Vandvik2020-hu; @wust2021interaction]. Grazing often removes biomass and can reduce the competition for light and nutrients and hence increase diversity [@Bernes2015-yg; @frank2005interactive]. We therefore propose that we could simplify and synthesize across multiple global change drivers by using community biomass as a *common currency*, which reflects the magnitude of their impacts on competitive interactions. If so, we predict that incorporating community biomass in models of community response to global change drivers eliminates the direct and interacting impact of those drivers (@fig-concept b).

![The working hypothesis that a) the three global change drivers warming, nitrogen addition and clipping (or grazing) affect plant diversity directly. By using b) community biomass as a *common currency* these direct effects can be eliminated and the three drivers operate through standing biomass on diversity.](figures/Figure1_hypotheses.png){#fig-concept width="600"}

We test this prediction using a fully factorial and crossed field experiment in montane Norwegian grasslands manipulating three common global change drivers: climate warming (transplant to lower elevation), nitrogen deposition (seven levels ranging between 0 and 100 kg N ha^-1^ y^-1^), grazing, and simulate grazing by clipping at two different intensities (@fig-methods). All three drivers are known to affect community biomass, composition and diversity. In ecosystems, where temperature is a limiting factor for productivity, a warmer climate will often result in increased plant growth, leading to more standing biomass [@elmendorf2012plot; @fazlioglu2021warming]. The increase in standing biomass often leads to a change in species composition and diversity, with a reduction in smaller alpine specialist species and an increase in taller species that are better competitors for light and nutrients, such as grasses and shrubs [@Vandvik2020-hu; @Alexander2015-gu; @lynn2023traits; @winkler2019responses]. In grassland vegetation, where plant growth and biomass is limited by nutrients, the specific effects of added nitrogen tends to be similar to those of increased temperature; increased growth, taller and denser vegetation, and intensified competition for light and nutrients[@yue2020changes; @Humbert2016-wg]. Accordingly, when grassland vegetation is exposed to both warming and nitrogen addition, both drivers have qualitatively similar effects on standing biomass and diversity [@yue2020changes]. In contrast to warming and nutrient addition, grazing animals affect plant communities primarily through removing biomass and acting as disturbance agents through grazing and trampling, although we note that their effects on productivity are complex as they also add nutrients addition from urine and dung. In productive systems, increased removal of biomass by grazers can lead to release from competitive interactions and hence increased diversity [@Austrheim2001-nu; @niedrist2009plant; @Bernes2015-yg; @frank2005interactive; @kaarlejarvi2017herbivores; @song2020grazing].

Plant communities responses to global change drivers often differ along environmental gradients and across habitats [@elmendorf2012plot; @Humbert2016-wg; @bjorkman2018plant; @Vandvik2020-hu; @milchunas1993quantitative]. To account for this context-dependency and how community responses are mediated through community biomass, we repeated the experiment in two different environments, an alpine and a sub-alpine grassland community. These montane grasslands in Norway are grazed by domestic and natural grazers with the extant grazing pressure decreasing with elevation [@halbritter2025effects]. The two sites represent different annual and growing season temperatures, with the alpine site being more temperature and nutrient limited (Supplementary Figures S1; REF ThreeD data paper). By replicating the experiment in two different environmental contexts we can test the generality of our hypothesis.

While we hypothesis that these global change drivers affect diversity and species composition mediated through standing biomass resulting in more competitive interactions (H1), alternative mechanisms are possible. First, warming can for example directly change vegetation composition due to local colonization and extinction [@Vandvik2020-hu; @bektacs2024colonization]. Second, increased nitrogen addition, in particular at high levels, can lead to acidic soil conditions [@tian2015global], which can lead to shifts in species composition and diversity. Finally, vegetation responses to grazing are complex, and species often either tolerate or avoid grazing [@archibald2019unified]. Such shifts in species composition might therefore not be mediated through community biomass. Ecological indicator values can be used to describe species community composition in response to environmental affinities and can provide further insights into the mechanisms of these dynamics [@diekmann2003species; @rumpf2018range], especially those not mediated through community biomass (H2).

Here we conducted a global change experiment in mountain grasslands, because they harbor unique biodiversity and provide important ecosystem functions and services such as carbon sequestration, water cycling, and grazing pastures; underpinning the lives and livelihoods of hundreds of millions of people [@egan2017mountain]. We used a fully factorial and crossed field experiment replicated across two sites, to test if global change drivers operate through the same mechansim on diversity and understanding alternative mechanisms. Plant communities moved to lower elevation experienced an approximately 3°C increase in average growing season temperature (air: 3.09 ± 0.186 °C, ground: 3.06 ± 0.176 °C, and soil: 2.82 ± 0.142 °C; Supplementary Figure S1, Table S1). We applied a large range of nitrogen levels to simulate nitrogen addition close to and well beyond the current atmospheric nitrogen deposition in the mountains in south-western Norway [@aas2023monitoring] (2-3 kg N ha^-1^ y^-1^) and the critical load for change in species composition in alpine grasslands [@bobbink2011review] (c. 5-10 kg N ha^-1^ y^-1^). Our understanding of environmentally extreme conditions is limited, and such simulations can provide a mechanistic understanding of thresholds for community change [@Kayler2015-pr]. We simulated grazing by clipping because our main interest was in the effect of biomass removal, however, we also had naturally grazed plots outside the fenced area to account for the difference between grazing by animals and clipping. After three years of global change treatments, we harvested standing biomass at peak growing season and assessed the change in vascular plant species composition and diversity.
